paragraphs.text: Late-onset Pompe disease (LOPD) is an autosomal recessive, progressive metabolic myopathy caused by partial deficiency of the lysosomal enzyme acid alpha-glucosidase (GAA), which leads to lysosomal glycogen accumulation. It can present any time from the first year of life to adulthood, as late as the sixth decade. Weakness mainly affects the trunk, proximal lower limb, and respiratory muscles. Classic infantile Pompe disease has residual enzyme activity below 1% and causes hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and early death. In contrast, the late-onset (juvenile and adult) form follows a more insidious course, and significant ventricular hypertrophy is not a typical feature (Forsha et al., 2011; Herbert et al., 2019; Jones et al., 2021).

paragraphs.text: Makos et al. (1987) reported 3 sons of healthy, nonconsanguineous parents who developed progressive proximal muscle weakness due to alpha-glucosidase deficiency. paragraphs.text: Forsha et al. (2011) evaluated cardiovascular findings in 87 patients with late-onset Pompe disease enrolled in a randomized trial of enzyme replacement therapy (median age 44 years; 51% men). At baseline, 46% of patients had at least 1 electrocardiographic or echocardiographic abnormality. ECG showed left ventricular hypertrophy in 12% and a short PR interval (90 to 120 ms) in 10%. On echocardiography, 7% had a left ventricular ejection fraction below 55% (range, 41 to 54%) and 5% had an elevated left ventricular mass index, all in the mild range. Bundle branch block and atrial enlargement were each found in 4%. Two patients had a history of Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome. There were no significant differences between patients with disease duration under 15 years and those with 15 years or more. Three of the patients whose symptoms began before age 10 years (60%) had at least 1 abnormality. The authors noted that the significant ventricular hypertrophy classically seen in infantile Pompe disease was absent, and that the abnormalities might be related to Pompe disease or to comorbid conditions.

paragraphs.text: Herbert et al. (2019) reviewed the charts of 84 patients with LOPD carrying the c.-32-13T-G variant. Four clinically diagnosed patients (4.8%), 2 male and 2 female, had symptom onset between 10 days and 20 months of age. Initial symptoms included delayed gross motor milestones, signs of proximal muscle weakness, swallowing and feeding difficulties, and sleep apnea. All patients had early, characteristic changes in posture and movement. Diagnosis was made between 10 and 26 months of age, a delay of 6 to 18 months. Additional findings included elevated creatine kinase (CK), ALT, and AST levels, PAS-positive vacuoles on muscle biopsy, myopathic facies, generalized or truncal hypotonia, hypernasality, Gowers sign, and myotonic discharges on EMG. Despite enzyme replacement therapy (ERT), musculoskeletal involvement progressed and residual muscle weakness persisted in all patients. This was shown by ptosis, myopathic facies, scoliosis, lumbar lordosis, scapular winging, and weakness of the trunk and lower extremities. One patient needed surgery for progressive thoracolumbar scoliosis at age 12 years. Echocardiograms and ECGs were normal in the patients described.
